title: “Good Source” vs “Excellent Source”: How Much Nutrient Do Those Claims Mean?

seo.title: Good Source vs Excellent Source: %DV
seo.meta_description: In U.S. labeling, “good source” generally means 10–19% of the Daily Value per reference amount; “high,” “rich in,” or “excellent source” means 20% DV or more.
seo.search_intent: Explain the legal U.S. thresholds behind good source and excellent source nutrient claims.

excerpt: On U.S. food labels, these are defined nutrient-content claims. “Good source” generally corresponds to 10–19% DV; “excellent source,” “high,” and “rich in” generally mean at least 20% DV.
content_html:
“Excellent source of calcium” sounds like marketing language, but in the United States it carries a numerical threshold. The wording tells you roughly where the food lands on the Daily Value scale.

Good source means a meaningful middle range

For nutrients covered by the rule, “good source,” “contains,” or “provides” generally means the food supplies 10–19% of the Daily Value per reference amount customarily consumed.

Excellent source begins at 20% DV

“High,” “rich in,” and “excellent source of” generally require 20% DV or more per reference amount. That is why the same food cannot casually move between “good” and “excellent” without the nutrient amount supporting the claim.

The claim applies to the named nutrient, not the whole food

A snack can be an excellent source of one vitamin and still be high in sodium or added sugar. Nutrient-content claims answer a narrow question about the named nutrient.

Check the serving and the %DV

The front claim is a shortcut; the Nutrition Facts panel shows the amount behind it. Use the claim to locate a nutrient quickly, then use %DV and the rest of the label to decide whether the whole product fits your needs.

faq.question: What percent DV is a good source?
faq.answer: Generally 10–19% of the Daily Value per reference amount for nutrients covered by the claim rules.

faq.question: What percent DV is an excellent source?
faq.answer: Generally 20% DV or more; “high” and “rich in” use the same threshold.

faq.question: Does excellent source mean the food is healthy overall?
faq.answer: No. The claim describes the named nutrient, not the entire nutrition profile.
